bank.prompt: Your chat UI converts each incoming text delta from markdown to HTML on its own and appends the result. Users sometimes see stray asterisks around words that should be bold, and code blocks render wrongly, but the final saved message is fine. Diagnose the cause and suggest a better approach.
bank.reference: Markdown syntax such as a pair of asterisks or a code fence often spans several deltas, so rendering each fragment alone sees an unmatched opening marker and shows it literally. The fix is to accumulate the full text so far and re-render that accumulated text on each update, or use a renderer designed for incremental input. Key points: formatting spans delta boundaries, and rendering must work on the accumulated text rather than on isolated fragments.

bank.prompt: You give the model a weather tool and stream the reply. The stream ends cleanly, the assembled text is empty, and the finish reason indicates a tool call. You did receive argument fragments for a tool call during the stream. What should your code do next?
bank.reference: A tool-call finish reason means the model deliberately stopped to ask you to run a tool; the turn is complete, not broken. You execute the call and return the result so the model can write its answer. Retrying treats a normal stop as an error, which wastes tokens and can loop forever.
options: Run the tool with the assembled arguments, send its result back in a follow-up request, and let the model continue
Treat the empty text as a failed generation and retry the same request until text comes back
Raise the maximum output tokens and retry, since an empty answer means the output was cut short
Show the assembled tool arguments to the user as the final answer, since that is what the model produced

bank.prompt: When your laptop calls the LLM API directly, text starts streaming within a second. In production, browsers reach your backend through a reverse proxy, and the whole answer appears at once after about 8 seconds. Your measured time to first token now roughly equals the total response time. What is the most likely cause?
bank.reference: When the first token arrives at the same moment as the last, something is holding the stream back, and reverse proxies commonly buffer whole responses by default. Disabling buffering for the streaming route, and flushing each event from your backend, restores incremental delivery. Longer prompts would raise time to first token, but text would still trickle in afterwards rather than all arriving together.
options: The proxy is buffering the response and only forwarding it when complete, so streaming must be unbuffered on that route
The production region runs a slower model deployment, which delays the first token by several seconds
The proxy's read timeout is too short, so it waits and retries before passing the response through
The prompts in production are much longer, so prompt processing delays everything until the end

bank.prompt: Your app has a stop button for long answers. Clicking it hides any further text, but your code keeps reading the stream quietly until it finishes. Token spend barely dropped after you added the button. What should the stop button do instead?
bank.reference: Closing the connection is how a client cancels a stream, which lets the server stop producing tokens you would otherwise pay for. Reading quietly to the end is tempting for collecting usage, but it means the full answer is still generated and billed. A separate request cannot reach the generation already in progress.
options: Abort the HTTP request so the connection closes and the server can stop generating
Keep reading in the background but discard the text, so usage numbers still arrive
Lower the maximum output tokens on the next request so answers end sooner
Send a second request telling the model to stop generating the current answer

bank.prompt: Your agent streams a payment tool call. The connection drops partway through the arguments, with no finish event. A lenient JSON repair library closes the open braces and gives a valid object containing a recipient and an amount of 10. What should the code do with this tool call?
bank.reference: Without a finish event you cannot know the arguments were complete; an amount of 10 could be the start of 1000, and the repair just hides the truncation. Only act on tool calls from a stream that finished normally. Successful parsing is the tempting trap, because valid JSON is not the same as complete JSON.
options: Discard it, since the arguments may be truncated, and retry the request instead of executing anything
Execute it, because the repaired arguments parsed successfully and contain every required field
Execute it, then ask the model in a follow-up request to confirm the amount was correct
Retry the request and append the new argument fragments onto the repaired partial arguments

modules.title: Rate limits and quotas
modules.objective: Work within request and token rate limits by reading limit signals and pacing traffic on the client side.

bank.prompt: Your account allows 500 requests per minute and 200,000 tokens per minute. A typical request uses about 1,500 input tokens and 500 output tokens. As traffic grows, which limit will you hit first?
bank.reference: Each request costs about 2,000 tokens, so \(200{,}000 / 2{,}000 = 100\) requests per minute exhausts the token budget long before 500 requests. The tempting mistake is to watch only the request count; input tokens count against token limits too, so long prompts make the token limit bind first.
options: The token limit, at roughly 100 requests per minute
The request limit, at 500 requests per minute
The request limit, because only output tokens count toward token limits
Both together, because the two limits are sized to match each other

bank.prompt: A response's rate limit headers show 470 of 500 requests remaining and 2,000 of 200,000 tokens remaining, with the token budget resetting in 30 seconds. Your next queued request has an 8,000 token prompt. What should a well-behaved client do?
bank.reference: The token budget, not the request budget, will reject this request, so the client should wait until enough tokens are available. Plenty of remaining requests is irrelevant when one request needs more tokens than remain, and sending anyway just produces a predictable 429.
options: Hold the request until the token budget has replenished enough to cover it
Send it now, since 470 remaining requests shows plenty of headroom
Send it now and rely on the retry loop if it comes back as a 429
Split the prompt into four 2,000 token requests and send them now

bank.prompt: The diagram shows five clients that all received a 429 at the same moment. Each then retries with exponential backoff and no jitter, sending attempts 1, 2 and 4 seconds after that first rejection. What is the problem with this pattern, and what fixes it?
bank.reference: Because every client computes the same deterministic delays, all retries arrive together and hit the limit again as a burst; randomizing each delay with jitter desynchronizes them. A cap or a larger base only changes when the clients collide, not whether they do.
options: Retries land in synchronized bursts; adding random jitter to each delay spreads them out
The delays grow too fast; a fixed one second delay would spread the load more evenly
The delays have no ceiling; adding a maximum delay cap stops the clients from colliding
The base delay is too small; starting at ten seconds removes the collisions entirely

bank.figure_alt: A timeline with five coloured client markers stacked at 0, 1, 2 and 4 seconds, showing when each client sends an attempt.

bank.prompt: A teammate argues that client-side pacing is pointless: just send requests as fast as possible and retry whenever a 429 comes back. Give two reasons why a client-side throttle that keeps traffic under the limit usually works better.
bank.reference: Look for at least two of: rejected requests waste round trips and add latency; reactive retries create bursts and retry storms that cause more 429s; tail latency becomes unpredictable; rejected attempts can still count against request limits; a throttle gives smooth, predictable throughput and lets you prioritize or queue work deliberately instead of discovering the limit by failing.

bank.prompt: Each request to the model takes about 10 seconds end to end. You want to sustain 120 requests per minute. Using \(L = \lambda W\), roughly how many requests must be in flight at the same time?
bank.reference: 120 requests per minute is \(\lambda = 2\) per second, and \(L = 2 \times 10 = 20\) requests in flight. The common slip is dividing 120 by 10 and mixing minutes with seconds, giving 12, or forgetting latency altogether.
options: About 20
About 12
About 2
About 120

bank.prompt: Your backoff policy says to wait 2 seconds before the next attempt, but the 429 response includes a retry-after header of 20 seconds. What should the client do, and why?
bank.reference: Wait at least the 20 seconds the server asked for, effectively using the larger of its own backoff and the retry-after value. The server knows when capacity will be available, so retrying sooner will most likely just produce another 429 and waste budget.

bank.prompt: The diagram shows your service after autoscaling from one replica to four. Each replica runs a local rate limiter set to 400k tokens per minute, matching the limit on the shared API key. Since scaling, 429s have spiked. What is the best fix?
bank.reference: Four limiters each allowing 400k tokens per minute can together send up to 1.6M against a 400k key, so the budget must be coordinated through a shared limiter or split across replicas. A small safety margin is tempting but still leaves the fleet allowed nearly four times the real limit.
options: Enforce the key's budget across replicas, with a shared limiter or a per-replica share
Raise each replica's retry count so rejected requests eventually succeed
Lower each local limiter slightly below 400k to leave a safety margin
Replace each local token limiter with a per-replica concurrency cap

bank.prompt: A classification job sends one item per request: a 600 token instruction block, a 50 token item and about 5 output tokens. You switch to 20 items per request, with the instructions included once. What happens to your rate limit usage for the same workload?
bank.reference: Twenty items now share one request, and the 600 token instructions are paid once instead of twenty times, so tokens per item fall from about 655 to about 85. The tempting answer assumes token use is unchanged, overlooking that the repeated instruction block dominated the old token count.
options: Requests per minute drop about twentyfold, and tokens per minute drop sharply too
Requests per minute drop about twentyfold, while tokens per minute stay about the same
Requests per minute drop, but tokens per minute rise because each request is larger
Neither changes much, because limits are measured per item rather than per request

bank.prompt: On a provider that counts each request's max_tokens against the token limit when the request is admitted, your app sets max_tokens to 4,000, but real replies average about 200 tokens. Predict what you will see as traffic grows, and what you should change.
bank.reference: You will hit the token limit far earlier than actual usage suggests, because each request reserves about 4,000 output tokens it never uses, so 429s appear while measured consumption looks low. Set max_tokens closer to realistic output lengths, with some headroom, to stop over-reserving budget.

bank.prompt: Twenty workers each read the remaining tokens header from their own latest response and send whenever it shows enough budget. They still hit frequent bursts of 429s. What is the most likely cause?
bank.reference: A header reflects the budget when that response was produced and cannot account for requests other workers have already sent; twenty workers seeing the same headroom all spend it at once. The fix is a shared limiter that tracks in-flight reservations rather than trusting per-worker snapshots.
options: Each worker's snapshot ignores requests other workers have in flight, so they overspend together
The headers describe usage from the previous minute, so every value lags a full window behind
Twenty workers exceed the provider's connection count, which triggers 429s regardless of budget
The reset value is read in the wrong unit, so workers wait far too long between sends

bank.prompt: Your service sends about 50,000 tokens per minute against a 300,000 token per minute limit, yet the remaining tokens header often shows under 20,000. What best explains this?
bank.reference: Rate limits are typically enforced at the organization, project or key level, so other services using the same scope draw down the shared budget the header reports. Tokenizer differences are real but cause small discrepancies, not a sixfold gap.
options: Other workloads share the same organization or project limit and are consuming most of it
The header counts tokens per second, so its values naturally look much smaller
The server tokenizes your prompts differently, inflating your counts about sixfold
The header resets only when traffic stops completely, so it drifts downward over time

bank.prompt: An interactive chat feature retries 429s with delays of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 seconds, so up to \(\sum_{k=0}^{5} 2^k\) seconds of waiting can pass before it gives up. Which change best fits this feature?
bank.reference: The schedule allows about 63 seconds of waiting, far beyond what a chat user will tolerate, so an interactive path should bound total retry time and fail fast with a fallback. Long schedules suit background jobs; a typing indicator hides the problem rather than fixing it.
options: Cap total retry time at a few seconds, then show a clear error or fallback
Keep the schedule but show a typing indicator so users tolerate the wait
Remove jitter so the user's retries happen at predictable, explainable times
Add more retries so the request almost never fails outright for the user

bank.prompt: The SDK retries a failed call twice with backoff, your wrapper retries the SDK call three times, and the job queue redelivers a failed job three times. During a rate limit incident, predict what happens to load on the API and suggest a fix.
bank.reference: Retries multiply across layers, so one logical call can become dozens of attempts, amplifying load exactly when the API is saturated and prolonging the 429s. Retry in one deliberate layer, or disable retries in the inner layers, and bound the total attempts and time.

bank.prompt: In the diagram, the client's token bucket starts full. Thirty requests arrive at the same moment, each spending one token, and requests wait while the bucket is empty. Assuming nothing else arrives, how are the thirty requests released?
bank.reference: The full bucket allows a burst of 20, then refills at 2 tokens per second, releasing the remaining 10 over about 5 seconds. Waiting for a full refill is the common misreading; a token bucket lets each request through as soon as a single token is available.
options: Twenty go immediately and the other ten trickle out over about five seconds
All thirty are spread evenly over about fifteen seconds at two per second
Twenty go immediately and the other ten are rejected as over capacity
Twenty go immediately and the rest wait about ten seconds for a full refill

bank.prompt: Your client caps in-flight requests at 10. During a peak, average model latency rises from 5 seconds to 20 seconds because replies get longer. Predict what happens to your throughput and whether you are likely to hit the requests per minute limit, and explain why.
bank.reference: With a fixed concurrency cap, throughput is concurrency divided by latency, so it falls from about 120 to about 30 requests per minute; the cap self-throttles, making request limit 429s unlikely. The cost is that work backs up in your queue, so latency for callers grows.

bank.prompt: You cap in-flight requests at 30, a value tuned when average latency was 15 seconds. After switching to a faster model with about 3 second latency, you start getting 429s on the requests per minute limit. Why?
bank.reference: Throughput under a concurrency cap is concurrency divided by latency, rising from about 120 to about 600 requests per minute here. A concurrency cap bounds simultaneous work, not rate, so it needs a rate limiter alongside it when latency can drop.
options: The same concurrency at a fifth of the latency sends about five times as many requests per minute
The cap leaks when requests finish quickly, letting far more than 30 run at once
Request limit 429s signal too many open connections, so the cap value is irrelevant
Faster replies use more tokens per request, which the provider reports as a request limit

modules.title: Error handling under real conditions
modules.objective: Classify API failures and apply the right response to each so that calls stay reliable in production code.

bank.prompt: Your integration sees four kinds of failed calls in one afternoon. Which one should your code retry automatically after a delay, with no change to the request?
bank.reference: A 429 is transient: the same request will succeed once the rate limit window allows it, so waiting and retrying is correct. The 400 and 401 errors are deterministic. The context-window 400 is the tempting one, but resending the same oversized prompt fails identically until the input is shortened.
options: A 429 rate limit error returned during a burst of traffic
A 400 error because a message has an invalid role field
A 401 error because the API key was revoked
A 400 error because the prompt exceeds the context window

bank.prompt: Your helper retries every exception up to 5 times with backoff. A request fails with a 400 because the prompt is longer than the model's context window. What will the retries achieve, and what should the code do instead?
bank.reference: Every retry fails the same way, because the request itself is invalid. That only adds latency and log noise. The code should classify 4xx validation errors like this as non-retryable and fail fast. It should then fix the input, for example by truncating, summarizing or chunking it, or surface a clear error.

bank.prompt: The diagram shows a non-streaming call with a 30 second client timeout. The server needs about a minute to generate the full answer, so every attempt times out. What is the right fix?
bank.reference: The timeout is shorter than the work itself, so every attempt fails no matter how often it is repeated. Streaming delivers tokens as they are generated, and a timeout sized to the expected output length also works. Adding retries or backoff is the tempting mistake: it repeats a request that cannot finish in time and may pay for the abandoned generations.
options: Stream the response, or raise the timeout to cover the longest expected generation
Increase the retry count so that one attempt eventually finishes in time
Add exponential backoff with jitter between the timed-out attempts
Lower the temperature so the model generates its answer faster

bank.prompt: A call returns HTTP 200, but the model's text politely declines to complete the task. How should your integration handle this response?
bank.reference: A refusal is a valid response about the content, not a transport or server failure. The code should recognize it and follow a planned path, such as a user-facing message, human review or a rephrased request. Blind retries are the common mistake: the same input usually produces the same refusal and multiplies cost.
options: Treat it as a successful call, detect the refusal, and return a defined fallback
Retry it with exponential backoff, since the refusal is likely transient
Raise it as a server error and page the on-call engineer
Resend the identical prompt at a higher temperature until it complies

bank.prompt: Your app asks the model for a JSON list and parses the reply. Parsing fails on about 2% of responses. All of the failures are unusually long, and each one reports a stop reason meaning the output token limit was reached. What is the right fix?
bank.reference: The stop reason shows the output was cut off, so the response is incomplete rather than malformed. Check the stop reason before parsing, and give the output enough token budget or split the work into smaller requests. Auto-repairing the JSON is tempting, but it silently drops data and hides the real cause.
options: Treat token-limit stops as incomplete, then raise max tokens or request smaller outputs
Repair the JSON by trimming the trailing fragment and closing any open brackets
Retry the identical request, since the next sample will likely be shorter
Lower the temperature so the model produces more consistent JSON formatting

bank.prompt: The diagram shows your code wrapping an SDK call in your own retry loop. The SDK also retries on its own, as the diagram shows. If the API keeps returning 503, what is the maximum number of HTTP requests a single user action can produce?
bank.reference: Each of your 4 attempts runs the SDK's full retry cycle of 1 request plus 2 retries, so the worst case is \(4 \times (1 + 2) = 12\) requests. Answering 4 or 6 is the common mistake. It forgets that the SDK retries automatically underneath your loop, so the two layers of retries multiply rather than add.

bank.prompt: A chat endpoint must show users either a first token or an error within 5 seconds. The SDK is left at its defaults, including automatic retries with backoff. During a provider incident, users wait far longer than 5 seconds before seeing anything. Explain why, and what you would change for this endpoint.
bank.reference: Each automatic retry adds another full attempt plus a backoff delay. A long default timeout also lets a single attempt hang well past the budget, so the total wait far exceeds 5 seconds. For this latency-sensitive path, set a short timeout and few or no retries, fail fast to a fallback such as an error message or alternate model, and keep generous retries for background work.

bank.prompt: The diagram shows your client's retries after a 429 response whose retry-after header said 20 seconds. Your backoff waited 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds between attempts. Every attempt failed, and the job then gave up. What should change?
bank.reference: The server said when capacity would be available, and every attempt before that point was guaranteed to fail and still counted against the limit. Honoring retry-after, then backing off with jitter, is the correct approach. Raising the retry limit is tempting because it eventually works by accident, but it still wastes requests during the blocked window.
options: Wait at least the retry-after duration before the next attempt
Shrink the backoff base so more attempts fit inside the window
Raise the retry limit so that later attempts land past 20 seconds
Send each retry to a different model to spread the load

bank.prompt: A batch job sends 50,000 documents through Anthropic's API. A few hundred requests fail with 400 because those documents are too long. A few hundred more fail with 529 overloaded during a busy hour. Describe how the pipeline should handle each group so the job still completes.
bank.reference: The 529 group is transient. Retry those requests with exponential backoff and jitter, possibly at lower concurrency or later in the run. The 400 group will fail identically if resent as-is. Do not retry them unchanged: send them to a dead-letter or review list, then chunk or truncate the documents and resubmit the modified requests.

bank.prompt: During a traffic spike, Anthropic's API returns 529 overloaded errors to your service. Your usage dashboard shows you are well under your rate limits. What is the most accurate interpretation?
bank.reference: A 529 means the API is temporarily overloaded across users. It is not a signal about your quota or your request, so backing off and retrying is appropriate. Confusing it with a 429 rate limit is the usual mistake, which sends people chasing quota increases that would not help.
options: The service is temporarily over capacity, so retry with backoff and jitter
Your organization exceeded its tokens-per-minute limit, so request more quota
The request body is too large, so split the prompt into smaller pieces
Your API key has been throttled, so rotate to a different key

bank.prompt: You set a 20 second client timeout and retry once on timeout. Afterward, billing shows output token usage for long requests roughly doubled, even though users received only one answer each. Explain the likely cause and how you would fix it.
bank.reference: The client timeout only stopped your side from waiting. The server likely kept generating and billed the first attempt, and then the retry started a second full generation, so you paid twice. The fix is to size the timeout to the expected generation length or use streaming, and to avoid retrying timeouts on requests that are known to be long.

bank.prompt: Your classifier retries up to 5 times whenever the reply lacks a valid label. For a small set of sensitive inputs, the model declines every time, so each of those inputs costs six calls and still fails. What is the best change?
bank.reference: Refusals on the same input are largely consistent, so retrying mostly multiplies cost. Recognize the refusal and route the input to a defined path, such as human review or an explicit 'unable to classify' result. Pushing temperature and retries is the tempting mistake: it treats a content decision as if it were random noise.
options: Detect refusals and send those inputs to a fallback path without retrying
Raise the retry limit and the temperature so a compliant sample appears
Increase max tokens so the model has enough room to produce the label
Switch to streaming so the label is captured before the model declines

bank.prompt: Explain how your code would detect two different outcomes: the model itself declining a request, and a provider-side safety filter blocking the output. Then explain why neither should go through the same retry path as a 5xx error.
bank.reference: A model refusal usually arrives as a normal successful response, so it must be detected from the content or from a refusal-type stop reason where the API provides one. A provider safety block is signalled explicitly, for example by a content-filter finish reason or a specific error. Both are about the input or output content rather than a transient fault, so an identical retry is unlikely to help. They need a fallback, a user message and logging instead.

bank.prompt: You request 40 records as JSON. Each record takes about 30 output tokens, and the surrounding JSON adds about 50 more. Max tokens is set to 1,000. Assuming the model follows your instruction, what should you expect?
bank.reference: The full output needs about \(40 \times 30 + 50 = 1250\) tokens, which exceeds the limit, so generation is cut off mid-structure and the stop reason reports the token limit. Max tokens is a hard cutoff on generation, not a target the model reliably plans around. Expecting the model to compress its answer to fit is the common mistake.
options: Output stops near 1,000 tokens, leaving invalid JSON and a token-limit stop reason
The model plans ahead and shortens records so the JSON closes within 1,000 tokens
The API rejects the request up front because the output cannot fit the limit
All of the roughly 1,250 tokens are returned, but billing is capped at 1,000 output tokens

bank.prompt: Your streaming handler saves whatever text has arrived when the stream closes. Support reports that some saved answers end mid-sentence. What check should run before an answer is saved as complete?
bank.reference: Only the terminal event with its stop reason tells you whether generation finished normally. A dropped connection, a mid-stream error or a token-limit stop all leave partial text behind. Checking the 200 status is the tempting mistake: in a stream the status is sent before generation starts, so it says nothing about how the stream ended.
options: Confirm the stream's final event arrived with a normal stop reason
Confirm the HTTP status was 200 when the stream first opened
Confirm the accumulated text is non-empty before saving it
Confirm the text ends with sentence-ending punctuation

bank.prompt: A serverless function with a 30 second execution limit calls an LLM through an SDK left at its defaults: a multi-minute request timeout and automatic retries. During a provider slowdown, invocations die with platform timeout errors, and your error handler never runs. What should you change?
bank.reference: The SDK's defaults are unaware of the platform's limit, so its waits and retries outlast the invocation and your handler never sees a clean error. Budget the timeout and retry count so all attempts plus backoff finish well under 30 seconds. Adding more retries is the tempting mistake, because it pushes the worst case even further past the limit.
options: Set the SDK timeout and retry count so the worst case fits inside 30 seconds
Keep the defaults, since the SDK adapts its timeout to the host's limits
Raise the retry count so transient failures get more chances within 30 seconds
Remove the timeout entirely and let the platform's 30 second limit enforce it
